summary: Describes the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), an XML-based client-server protocol for provisioning objects in a shared central repository, such as domain registries. It defines generic operations and a framework for mapping them to object types. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: EPP gives clients and servers a shared XML format for managing objects in a central repository. Its generic commands work with separate object mappings, which define the details for objects such as domain names.

questions: how do registrars talk to domain registries
how does epp transfer a domain
how does an epp session work
subtitle: The XML client-server framework for managing objects in a shared repository.

tldr.problem: Different service providers need a common way to manage objects held in a shared repository, while repositories may define different object types.
tldr.mechanism: EPP exchanges XML greetings, commands, and responses in a stateful session. A base set of commands handles sessions and generic operations; separate object mappings define object-specific data.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5730 is Internet Standard STD 69 and obsoletes RFC 4930. It defines the extensible base protocol, not a particular object's mapping or a specific transport binding.

today: RFC 5730 is Internet Standard STD 69, published in August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4930; object details such as domain names are defined in separate mappings, including RFC 5731.

sections.title: The Purpose and Scope of EPP
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) lets multiple service providers manage objects in a shared central repository. Its original motivation was to provide a standard protocol between domain name registrars and registries, but the RFC anticipates other uses. EPP version 1.0 uses XML and identifies its content with the media type application/epp+xml.

EPP is designed for different operating environments. A transport mapping must preserve command order and protocol state, frame data, provide reliability and congestion avoidance, and state whether pipelining is allowed. This RFC defines no binding to a specific transport or security protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP gives clients and repository servers a common way to exchange management requests. The protocol defines the shared message structure, while a separate mapping explains the details for each kind of object.

sections.title: Sessions, Commands, and Processing
sections.content:
EPP is stateful: a client and server establish a session, then exchange client-initiated commands and server responses. The server sends a greeting when a client connects or sends <hello>. A successful <login> must precede other commands, and <logout> ends the session.

Commands fall into session-management, query, and object-transform groups. The server processes commands in the order received. Commands are atomic: an operation either succeeds completely or fails completely. They are designed to be idempotent, so repeating one has the same effect as executing it once. A transform may be accepted but remain pending while offline work is completed; the server must notify the client when that work finishes.
sections.plainLanguage: A client first opens a session and logs in, then sends commands that the server answers in order. Each command has one complete result, and some changes may remain pending until the server finishes separate work.

sections.title: XML Greetings, Commands, and Responses
sections.content:
Every EPP message uses an <epp> root element in the EPP XML namespace. A greeting identifies the server, gives its current time, lists supported versions, languages, object types and extensions, and includes a data-collection policy. A command contains an EPP command, optional extension data, and may contain a client transaction identifier.

A response includes a result code and human-readable message, and may include queued-message information, object-specific response data, or extensions. Its transaction identifier combines the client's identifier, when supplied, with a server-assigned identifier. Date-time values use UTC; UTF-8 is the recommended encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The greeting tells the client what the server supports. Each response reports the result and carries identifiers that let both sides match it to the command.

sections.title: Object Mappings and Extensions
sections.content:
The base EPP protocol does not define managed objects. Object-specific information is identified with XML namespaces and schemas, so a new mapping can add an object without changing the base protocol. A separate mapping document must describe the commands and responses for that object; RFC 5731 is the domain name mapping.

EPP also supports protocol extensions and optional command-response extension elements. Extensions can add features, object mappings can define object data, and a server and client may agree to operational extensions. Every object must receive a globally unique identifier when it is created, and an info response returns that identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The base protocol supplies common commands but no object definitions. Separate mappings add the fields and responses for each object type, without requiring a new base protocol.

sections.title: Queries, Changes, and Service Messages
sections.content:
Query commands retrieve information: <check> gives a hint about whether an object can be provisioned, <info> returns object details, and <poll> retrieves queued service messages. Transform commands create, delete, renew, transfer, or update objects. Object mappings supply the object-specific fields for these operations.

A client acknowledges a retrieved poll message before the next queued message becomes available. A transfer request changes which client sponsors an object; the current sponsor may approve or reject it, and the server may apply a documented default after a period of inactivity. Object-specific authorization information is required to complete an eligible transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Queries read object information, while transform commands request changes. The object mapping defines what information each command needs, and queued notices tell clients about service events.

sections.title: Four-Digit Result Codes
sections.content:
Every EPP response includes a four-digit decimal result code and a human-readable description. The first digit distinguishes positive completion (1yzz) from negative completion (2yzz), where the requested action did not occur. The second digit identifies a response category: protocol syntax, implementation-specific rules, security, data management, server system, or connection management.

The final two digits give detail within the category. Response text may be translated, but the numeric code must keep its defined meaning. If a response is missing or malformed, the client must not assume that the command succeeded or failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The first digit tells whether the command completed positively or negatively. The next digit groups the result by issue type, and the last two add detail.

sections.title: Security Comes from Lower Layers
sections.content:
EPP's own login sends the client identifier and password in separate XML elements. A passive observer can recover both, so EPP instances must use a transport or application protocol that provides integrity, confidentiality, and strong mutual client-server authentication.

Idempotency and transaction identifiers reduce some replay risks, but a repeated command after intervening changes can still have an unintended effect. Authorization data used for object transfers must be protected in transit. Notifications sent outside the secured EPP connection need their own appropriate protection.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP's password exchange is not safe to expose on an unprotected connection. Another protocol layer must encrypt and protect the connection and authenticate both sides.
